---
title: "Serialised specifications"
subtitle: "Reaching the pipeline from a generator in another language."
description: "display-table(spec:), the JSON subset it accepts, and the keys a serialised Keisen specification can carry."
---

`display-table(spec: ..)` renders a specification instead of data and directives, which is how a generator in another language reaches this pipeline without emitting table markup.
A specification that arrives as data, from `json()` or from a tool, cannot carry closures, so it names what it wants:

```json
{
  "kind": "display-table",
  "data": [{"product": "Bolt", "region": "North", "units": 1250, "margin": 0.182}],
  "header": {"title": "Regional sales"},
  "stub": {"rowname": "product", "group": "region"},
  "formats": [{"name": "format-integer", "columns": "units"}],
  "summaries": [{"name": "aggregate-sum", "label": "Subtotal", "columns": ["units"]}],
  "styles": [
    {
      "style": {"text": {"weight": "bold"}},
      "part": "body",
      "columns": "margin",
      "rows": {"column": "margin", "op": "<", "value": 0.05}
    }
  ]
}
```

Formatters and aggregations are named from the built-ins, and row predicates are comparisons with `op` in `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `==`, `!=`, composed with `and`, `or`, and `not`.
Comparing against `null` asks whether the cell is empty, which is the only way JSON has to spell absence.
Every key is checked, inside a descriptor as well as at the top level, so a misspelled `columns` fails rather than quietly widening what it applies to.
That is the whole subset: no arithmetic, no function calls, no set tests.
Anything more expressive belongs in a Typst specification, which keeps the schema from drifting into an expression language.

A combine pattern arrives the same way, as a template rather than a closure: `"{1} ({2})"`, numbering the sources from one in `from` order.

## What the subset reaches

| Key | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| `kind` | `"display-table"`. |
| `data` | Rows or columns, as `display-table` takes them. |
| `header` | `title` and `subtitle`. |
| `stub` | `rowname`, `group`, `label`, `indent`. |
| `row-groups` | Descriptors of `label` and `rows`. |
| `labels` | Column name to label. |
| `hidden` | A column name or an array of them. |
| `combines` | `into`, `from`, `pattern`, `label`, `hide-sources`. |
| `moves` | `columns`, and one of `before` or `after`. |
| `spanners` | `label`, `columns`, `level`. |
| `widths` | Column name to a width written as a string. |
| `alignments` | Descriptors of `alignment` and `columns`. |
| `formats` | Descriptors naming a formatter, with its own options. |
| `substitutions` | `test`, `columns`, `rows`, `replacement`. |
| `colours` | `palette`, `columns`, `rows`, `domain`, `target`, `missing`, `reverse`. |
| `summaries` | `name`, `label`, `columns`, `groups`. |
| `grand-summaries` | The same, over the whole body. |
| `styles` | A `style` dictionary and the location keys below. |
| `footnotes` | `note`, `locations`, `mark`. |
| `source-notes` | An array of strings. |
| `options` | Theme options, merged over the theme the caller gave. |

: Serialised keys {.striped .hover tbl-colwidths="[25,75]"}

A location is written with `part`, `columns`, `rows`, `groups`, `spanners`, `notes` and `parts`, and a style and a footnote address cells the same way.

The nameable formatters are `format-number`, `format-integer`, `format-percent`, `format-currency`, `format-scientific`, `format-bytes`, `format-date` and `format-markup`.
The formatters that cannot be named are `format`, `format-cell` and `format-nanoplot`: each is given a function, and JSON has no way to write one, so they are absent by nature rather than by omission.

The nameable aggregations are `aggregate-sum`, `aggregate-mean`, `aggregate-median`, `aggregate-min`, `aggregate-max`, `aggregate-count` and `aggregate-standard-deviation`.
Not every aggregation can be named: `aggregate-quantile` takes a probability and returns the aggregation, so naming it would mean calling it.

A width is a string carrying a number and one of `pt`, `mm`, `cm`, `in`, `em`, `fr` or `%`, or `"auto"`.
A bare number is refused rather than given a unit nobody wrote.
An alignment is one of `start`, `end`, `center`, `left` or `right`.
Its `columns` is a name, an array of names, or `null` for every column.
JSON writes no predicate, so an array is the only way a generator names several columns, and every name in it is held to the table: one the table does not carry is reported rather than skipped.
A colour is a hex string, wherever one is wanted: a palette stop, a fill, a text fill, or the colour a missing value takes.

A `style` carries the same five properties `style()` takes, each written as JSON can write it.

| Property | Written as |
| --- | --- |
| `fill` | A colour. |
| `text` | A dictionary Typst reads, with `fill` as a colour and `size` as a length. |
| `align` | A horizontal name, a vertical name of `top`, `horizon` or `bottom`, or the two added: `"center + horizon"`. |
| `inset` | A length, or a dictionary of `left`, `right`, `top`, `bottom`, `x`, `y` or `rest`, each a length. |
| `stroke` | A colour, a length for the thickness, `null` for no rule, or a dictionary of `paint`, `thickness` and whatever else Typst reads, such as `dash`. |

: Style properties {.striped .hover tbl-colwidths="[25,75]"}

`tests/unit/test-serialised-surface.typ` holds this page to the tables the resolver reads, so a name added to one and not the other fails the suite.

A serialised specification is turned back into ordinary directives and folded through the same path as a hand-written table, so the two cannot diverge: one pipeline, entered two ways.
`examples/serialised.typ` renders `examples/table-spec.json` and compiles with the test suite.
